props.title: Shankesh Jewellers IPO — at a Glance
items: Business: B2B, asset-light handcrafted gold jewellery (Mumbai)

props.closer: A capital-efficient, fast-growing wholesale jeweller — but with no clean peer and a model whose margins must prove durable. Read the RHP; decide for yourself.

captions: Let's break down the Shankesh Jewellers I-P-O —
a three hundred and sixty-seven crore mainboard issue with an unusual,
asset-light business model and explosive recent profit growth.
We'll cover what it does, its full financials,
where the money goes, how to think about its valuation,
and whether it fits you.
This is education, not investment advice.
So what does Shankesh do?
It designs, sources and supplies customised,
handcrafted twenty-two and eighteen-karat gold jewellery —
largely a business-to-business, wholesale model.
And here's the unusual part: it's asset-light.
It does not run its own factory.
Instead it works through a network of about seventy-two skilled karigars,
or jobworkers, while keeping control of design, sourcing,
quality and finishing.
It's Mumbai-based, founded in two thousand five.
So think of it as a design-and-supply house, not a factory.
Now the financials — and the profit growth is striking.
Total income rose to about one thousand six hundred and thirty-one crore in FY twenty twenty-six.
But look at profit: it surged over a hundred and sixty-four percent —
from about forty crore to a hundred and seven crore.
And the returns are exceptional —
a return on equity near fifty-one percent,
and return on capital around forty-two percent.
That's the asset-light model at work —
high returns because it doesn't tie up money in factories.
Let's put all three statements together.
The income statement shows income of about sixteen hundred crore and profit of a hundred and seven crore,
on a healthy six and a half percent margin.
The balance sheet is where the model shines —
return on equity near fifty-one percent,
because it carries little more than about a hundred and sixty-seven crore of debt and no big factory.
On cash flow, the fresh money —
about a hundred and fifty-eight crore — repays debt,
and thirty-eight crore funds working capital.
The full operating cash-flow line isn't published in the summaries —
read the R-H-P.
Where does your money go?
Of the three hundred and sixty-seven crore issue,
about two hundred and seventy-four crore —
roughly seventy-five percent — is a fresh issue,
money going into the company.
The remaining ninety-three crore is an Offer for Sale,
where the Jain promoters sell part of their stake.
So it's a mostly-fresh issue —
three-quarters funds the business.
That's a healthy structure.
What does the fresh money fund?
The largest use — about a hundred and fifty-eight crore —
repays borrowings,
cutting finance costs and de-risking a fast-growing business.
Another thirty-eight crore funds working capital —
gold inventory and order flow,
the lifeblood of a design-and-supply jeweller.
And the rest goes to general corporate purposes.
A sensible, deleveraging use of the money.
So how is it priced against rivals?
Here's the honest complication: there's no clean listed twin.
Big names like Kalyan or Titan are consumer retail brands with their own stores; Shankesh is a business-to-business,
asset-light wholesaler — a genuinely different model,
so a simple P/E comparison can mislead.
What you can say is that its growth and returns —
profit up a hundred and sixty-four percent,
a fifty-one percent return on equity —
are far above sector norms, which justifies some premium.
But explosive growth like that is hard to repeat.
The real question is whether a wholesale,
jobworker-based model can sustain these margins as it grows.
Judge it on that.
So — should you subscribe?
The strengths are eye-catching —
profit up a hundred and sixty-four percent,
a fifty-one percent return on equity,
an asset-light and capital-efficient model,
and three-quarters of the issue is fresh money that also cuts debt.
The watch-outs are just as important —
there's no clean listed peer to benchmark the price against; it's a business-to-business wholesaler,
which brings thinner margins and key-customer risk; and you have to ask whether such explosive growth can be sustained.
The takeaway — a fast-growing,
efficient niche business at a fair-looking price,
but one that's harder to value and to predict.
Only you can decide.
Finally — how do you apply, and how much?
Retail investors bid up to two lakh for a thirty-five percent quota,
with allotment by lottery if oversubscribed.
H-N-Is bid above two lakh for a fifteen percent quota.
For Shankesh, at an eighty-eight to ninety-three rupee band,
one lot works out to about fifteen thousand rupees —
your minimum.
Track the live subscription on the N-S-E and B-S-E I-P-O pages,
Chittorgarh, Moneycontrol, or your broker app.
Let's recap Shankesh Jewellers.
An asset-light,
business-to-business handcrafted-gold-jewellery house from Mumbai —
profit exploded a hundred and sixty-four percent,
with a fifty-one percent return on equity.
The issue is about seventy-five percent fresh,
mainly repaying debt.
The catch is valuation and durability —
there's no clean listed peer,
and you must ask whether a wholesale model can sustain these margins.
The retail minimum is about fifteen thousand rupees.
This video explains the IPO for education only —
it is not investment advice,
not a buy or sell recommendation,
and not a prediction of listing gains.
Grey-market premium is unofficial and changes hourly.
Always read the RHP and check the live subscription before you apply.
Thanks for watching.
